authors: Bruffaerts, R., Mortier, P., Kiekens, G., Auerbach, R. P., Cuijpers, P., Demyttenaere, K., Green, J. G., Nock, M. K., & Kessler, R. C.
title: Mental health problems in college freshmen: Prevalence and academic functioning
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: Web survey, WMH-ICS; n = 4,921 first-year students, KU Leuven (Belgium)
key finding: About one in three KU Leuven freshmen reported a 12-month mental health problem, and these problems were linked to a 2.9–4.7% lower academic year percentage (0.2–0.3 GPA points).
limitations: Cross-sectional; self-report screening; no data on prior secondary-school performance; causality not established (authors).

authors: Auerbach, R. P., Mortier, P., Bruffaerts, R., Alonso, J., Benjet, C., Cuijpers, P., Demyttenaere, K., Ebert, D. D., Green, J. G., Hasking, P., Murray, E., Nock, M. K., Pinder-Amaker, S., Sampson, N. A., Stein, D. J., Vilagut, G., Zaslavsky, A. M., & Kessler, R. C., on behalf of the WHO WMH-ICS Collaborators
title: WHO World Mental Health Surveys International College Student Project: Prevalence and distribution of mental disorders
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: Web surveys in 19 colleges, 8 countries incl. Belgium; n = 13,984 full-time first-year students; 45.5% pooled response rate
key finding: 35% screened positive for at least one lifetime and 31% for at least one 12-month common mental disorder.
limitations: Screening scales, not clinical diagnosis; under half of invited students responded; correlates were modest (authors).

authors: Auerbach, R. P., Alonso, J., Axinn, W. G., Cuijpers, P., Ebert, D. D., Green, J. G., Hwang, I., Kessler, R. C., Liu, H., Mortier, P., Nock, M. K., Pinder-Amaker, S., Sampson, N. A., Aguilar-Gaxiola, S., Al-Hamzawi, A., Andrade, L. H., Benjet, C., Caldas-de-Almeida, J. M., Demyttenaere, K., . . . Bruffaerts, R.
title: Mental disorders among college students in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: WHO WMH household surveys, 21 countries; n = 1,572 college students vs 4,178 non-students aged 18–22 (CIDI interviews)
key finding: 20.3% of college students had a 12-month disorder, 83.1% of these began before entering college, and only 16.4% received any professional care for it in the past year.
limitations: Older data pooled across very different countries; student subsample modest; interview-based estimates (authors' design).

authors: Mason, A., Rapsey, C., Sampson, N., Lee, S., Albor, Y., Al-Hadi, A. N., Alonso, J., Al-Saud, N., Altwaijri, Y., Andersson, C., Atwoli, L., Auerbach, R. P., Ayuya, C., Báez-Mansur, P. M., Ballester, L., Bantjes, J., Baumeister, H., Bendtsen, M., Benjet, C., . . . Bruffaerts, R.
title: Prevalence, age-of-onset, and course of mental disorders among 72,288 first-year university students from 18 countries in the World Mental Health International College Student (WMH-ICS) initiative
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: Online screening surveys 2017–2023; n = 72,288 first-year students, 77 universities, 18 countries; weighted response rate 20.8%
key finding: 65.2% screened positive for a lifetime and 57.4% for a 12-month mental disorder (DSM-5 screening scales).
limitations: Authors state prevalence may be overestimated because of the low response rate and possible screening-scale miscalibration.

authors: Nuijen, J., Busch, M., Winkens, K., Verweij, A., Dopmeijer, J., Buijs, M., Korteling, S., Boekee, R., Smits, R., & van den Brink, C.
title: Monitor Mentale gezondheid en Middelengebruik Studenten hbo en wo 2025 (RIVM-rapport 2025-0106)
journal: Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu (RIVM) & Trimbos-instituut
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: National online survey, spring 2025; n = 27,446 students at 23 Dutch institutions (12 hbo, 11 wo); 5.9% of the 466,313 enrolled students took part
key finding: Five of ten mental health measures improved since 2021, yet only 23% of students were flourishing, and 53% of students with psychological problems who did not seek support within their institution said they preferred to solve problems themselves.
limitations: Very low participation (5.9%); self-report; repeated cross-sections rather than following the same students; most improvements were small (authors).

authors: Abraham, A., Chaabna, K., Sheikh, J. I., Mamtani, R., Jithesh, A., Khawaja, S., & Cheema, S.
title: Burnout increased among university students during the COVID-19 pandemic: A systematic review and meta-analysis
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: Systematic review and meta-analysis; 44 studies, 26,500 university students, pandemic period
key finding: Pooled prevalence was 56.3% for high emotional exhaustion, 55.3% for high cynicism and 41.8% for low personal accomplishment.
limitations: Pandemic-period data only; substantial heterogeneity; certainty of evidence rated moderate (authors).

authors: Hara, Y., Furuta, S., Sukegawa, A., Fujimaki, K., & Hisano, S.
title: Systematic review of student burnout instruments: No measures currently meet COSMIN standards for recommendation
claim_area: a. Prevalence and burden
sample/design: COSMIN systematic review; 44 studies, 33 self-report student burnout measures
key finding: No student burnout questionnaire met COSMIN criteria for recommendation: 10 were rated 'recommend against' and 23 'no conclusion'.
limitations: Review of measurement quality only; does not estimate prevalence.

authors: Ebert, D. D., Mortier, P., Kaehlke, F., Bruffaerts, R., Baumeister, H., Auerbach, R. P., Alonso, J., Vilagut, G., Martínez, K. U., Lochner, C., Cuijpers, P., Kuechler, A.-M., Green, J., Hasking, P., Lapsley, C., Sampson, N. A., & Kessler, R. C., on behalf of the WHO World Mental Health–International College Student Initiative collaborators
title: Barriers of mental health treatment utilization among first-year college students: First cross-national results from the WHO World Mental Health International College Student Initiative
journal: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research
claim_area: b. Help-seeking, stigma and barriers
sample/design: WMH-ICS web surveys; n = 13,984 first-year students, 8 countries incl. Belgium
key finding: Only 24.6% said they would definitely seek help for a future emotional problem; the most common reasons not to were wanting to handle it alone (56.4%) and preferring to talk to friends or family (48.0%).
limitations: Help-seeking intention, not observed behaviour; self-report (authors call for experimental research).

authors: Gulliver, A., Griffiths, K. M., & Christensen, H.
title: Perceived barriers and facilitators to mental health help-seeking in young people: A systematic review
claim_area: b. Help-seeking, stigma and barriers
sample/design: Systematic review; 22 studies (15 qualitative, 7 quantitative) of adolescents and young adults
key finding: Young people named stigma and embarrassment, difficulty recognising symptoms, and a preference for self-reliance as the main barriers to seeking help.
limitations: Small, mostly qualitative evidence base; facilitators under-researched (authors); not student-specific.

authors: Clement, S., Schauman, O., Graham, T., Maggioni, F., Evans-Lacko, S., Bezborodovs, N., Morgan, C., Rüsch, N., Brown, J. S. L., & Thornicroft, G.
title: What is the impact of mental health-related stigma on help-seeking? A systematic review of quantitative and qualitative studies
claim_area: b. Help-seeking, stigma and barriers
sample/design: Systematic review; 144 studies, 90,189 participants
key finding: Stigma had a small-to-moderate negative association with help-seeking (median d = −0.27) and ranked fourth among barriers, with youth among the groups most deterred.
limitations: Mixed study designs; searches to 2011; not student-specific.

authors: Lindsay, J. A. B., McGowan, N. M., King, N., Rivera, D., Li, M., Byun, J., Cunningham, S., Saunders, K. E. A., & Duffy, A.
title: Psychological predictors of insomnia, anxiety and depression in university students: Potential prevention targets
claim_area: c. Sleep and activity as early indicators
sample/design: Longitudinal surveys at entry and end of first year; two cohorts at Queen's University, Canada (n = 1,519 and n = 860)
key finding: Insomnia symptoms at university entry predicted depressive (β = 0.15) and anxiety (β = 0.16) symptoms at year end, after controlling for baseline symptoms.
limitations: Self-report; self-selected sample, more female (74% vs 58%), cisgender only; attrition in cohort 2 during COVID-19 (authors).

authors: Hertenstein, E., Feige, B., Gmeiner, T., Kienzler, C., Spiegelhalder, K., Johann, A., Jansson-Fröjmark, M., Palagini, L., Rücker, G., Riemann, D., & Baglioni, C.
title: Insomnia as a predictor of mental disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis
claim_area: c. Sleep and activity as early indicators
sample/design: Meta-analysis of 13 longitudinal studies, follow-up ≥ 12 months
key finding: Insomnia at baseline predicted later onset of depression (OR 2.83, 10 studies) and anxiety (OR 3.23, 6 studies).
limitations: Few studies per outcome, wide confidence intervals, moderate risk of bias (authors); general population, not students.

authors: Schuch, F. B., Vancampfort, D., Firth, J., Rosenbaum, S., Ward, P. B., Silva, E. S., Hallgren, M., Ponce De Leon, A., Dunn, A. L., Deslandes, A. C., Fleck, M. P., Carvalho, A. F., & Stubbs, B.
title: Physical activity and incident depression: A meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
claim_area: c. Sleep and activity as early indicators
sample/design: Meta-analysis of 49 prospective cohort studies, N = 266,939
key finding: People with high physical activity had lower odds of developing depression than those with low activity (adjusted OR 0.83; youths 0.90).
limitations: Observational, so causality is not established; publication bias detected, although adjustment did not change the estimate (authors).

authors: Scott, A. J., Webb, T. L., Martyn-St James, M., Rowse, G., & Weich, S.
title: Improving sleep quality leads to better mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
local_file: Scott_2021_SleepQualityMentalHealth.pdf (open access, not downloaded: see NOTES.md)
claim_area: c. Sleep and activity as early indicators
sample/design: Meta-analysis of 65 RCTs (72 interventions), N = 8,608
key finding: Interventions that improved sleep had a medium effect on composite mental health (g = −0.53), with a dose–response relationship.
limitations: Mixed populations and sleep interventions, mostly not app-based or student-specific.

authors: Freeman, D., Sheaves, B., Goodwin, G. M., Yu, L.-M., Nickless, A., Harrison, P. J., Emsley, R., Luik, A. I., Foster, R. G., Wadekar, V., Hinds, C., Gumley, A., Jones, R., Lightman, S., Jones, S., Bentall, R., Kinderman, P., Rowse, G., Brugha, T., . . . Espie, C. A.
title: The effects of improving sleep on mental health (OASIS): A randomised controlled trial with mediation analysis
claim_area: c. Sleep and activity as early indicators
sample/design: RCT at 26 UK universities; 3,755 students with insomnia, digital CBT for insomnia vs usual care
key finding: Digital CBT-I reduced insomnia strongly (d = 1.11) and also reduced depression (d = 0.48) and anxiety (d = 0.33) at 10 weeks.
limitations: Students with insomnia only; online self-report; dropout higher than planned (authors increased the sample).

authors: Wang, R., Chen, F., Chen, Z., Li, T., Harari, G., Tignor, S., Zhou, X., Ben-Zeev, D., & Campbell, A. T.
title: StudentLife: Assessing mental health, academic performance and behavioral trends of college students using smartphones
journal: Proceedings of the 2014 ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp '14)
local_file: Wang_2014_StudentLife.pdf (open access, not downloaded: see NOTES.md)
claim_area: d. Passive sensing and daily check-ins
sample/design: Observational; 48 undergraduates, one 10-week term, continuous phone sensing plus about 8 EMA prompts per day
key finding: Phone-sensed sleep duration (r = −0.36) and daytime conversation frequency (r = −0.40) correlated with depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) at the start of term.
limitations: 48 students in one class at one US college; correlational; engagement and data quality fell over the term (authors).

authors: Rohani, D. A., Faurholt-Jepsen, M., Kessing, L. V., & Bardram, J. E.
title: Correlations between objective behavioral features collected from mobile and wearable devices and depressive mood symptoms in patients with affective disorders: Systematic review
claim_area: d. Passive sensing and daily check-ins
sample/design: Systematic review; 46 studies, 85 behavioural features from 17 sensor types
key finding: Time at home, sleep duration and vigorous activity correlated consistently with mood across studies, while other features (texting, screen use) pointed in contradictory directions.
limitations: Patients with affective disorders, not students; no standardisation of features, mood measures or statistics (authors).

authors: Müller, S. R., Chen, X. L., Peters, H., Chaintreau, A., & Matz, S. C.
title: Depression predictions from GPS-based mobility do not generalize well to large demographically heterogeneous samples
claim_area: d. Passive sensing and daily check-ins
sample/design: Secondary analysis; student sample N = 57 vs US-wide sample N = 5,262
key finding: A GPS-based depression model that looked accurate in a small student sample (AUC 0.82) was only slightly better than chance in a large mixed sample (AUC 0.57).
limitations: GPS mobility features only; US data.

authors: Adler, D. A., Wang, F., Mohr, D. C., & Choudhury, T.
title: Machine learning for passive mental health symptom prediction: Generalization across different longitudinal mobile sensing studies
claim_area: d. Passive sensing and daily check-ins
sample/design: Secondary analysis combining StudentLife (students) and CrossCheck (schizophrenia) sensing data
key finding: Models trained on combined datasets were more often predictive than single-study models, but personalisation helped only one outcome and boosting sensitivity cost specificity.
limitations: Two public datasets; only sleep quality and stress outcomes were comparable.

authors: Wrzus, C., & Neubauer, A. B.
title: Ecological momentary assessment: A meta-analysis on designs, samples, and compliance across research fields
claim_area: d. Passive sensing and daily check-ins
sample/design: Meta-analysis; 477 articles, 496 samples, N = 677,536
key finding: EMA studies averaged six prompts a day over seven days with 79% compliance; the number of prompts did not predict compliance, while financial incentives raised it.
limitations: Research studies of about a week, often paid; not real-world app use over a semester.

authors: Harrer, M., Adam, S. H., Baumeister, H., Cuijpers, P., Karyotaki, E., Auerbach, R. P., Kessler, R. C., Bruffaerts, R., Berking, M., & Ebert, D. D.
title: Internet interventions for mental health in university students: A systematic review and meta-analysis
journal: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research
claim_area: e. Brief digital self-help and exercises
sample/design: Meta-analysis of 48 RCTs in university students
key finding: Effects were small for depression (g = 0.18) and stress (g = 0.20); anxiety (g = 0.27) lost significance after adjusting for publication bias, and well-being was not significant (g = 0.15).
limitations: Only 48% of studies at low risk of bias; moderate-to-substantial heterogeneity (authors).

authors: Linardon, J., Torous, J., Firth, J., Cuijpers, P., Messer, M., & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M.
title: Current evidence on the efficacy of mental health smartphone apps for symptoms of depression and anxiety. A meta-analysis of 176 randomized controlled trials
claim_area: e. Brief digital self-help and exercises
sample/design: Meta-analysis of 176 RCTs
key finding: Apps had small but significant effects on depression (g = 0.28, NNT 11.5) and generalised anxiety (g = 0.26, NNT 12.4), larger when they included CBT elements or, for anxiety, mood monitoring.
limitations: Mixed populations; many secondary outcomes based on small, high-risk-of-bias trials (authors).

authors: Lattie, E. G., Adkins, E. C., Winquist, N., Stiles-Shields, C., Wafford, Q. E., & Graham, A. K.
title: Digital mental health interventions for depression, anxiety, and enhancement of psychological well-being among college students: Systematic review
claim_area: e. Brief digital self-help and exercises
sample/design: Systematic review; 89 studies in college students
key finding: 47% of programmes were effective and 34% partially effective, but half of the studies reported no usability or acceptability data and only 4% examined campus-wide implementation.
limitations: Moderate-to-severe risk of bias in many studies; mostly web-based programmes (80%) (authors).

authors: Weisel, K. K., Fuhrmann, L. M., Berking, M., Baumeister, H., Cuijpers, P., & Ebert, D. D.
title: Standalone smartphone apps for mental health—A systematic review and meta-analysis
claim_area: e. Brief digital self-help and exercises
sample/design: Meta-analysis; 19 RCTs, 3,681 adults with elevated symptoms
key finding: Standalone apps improved depression (g = 0.33) but showed no significant pooled effect on anxiety, and the authors concluded standalone apps cannot yet be recommended.
limitations: Few trials per outcome; heterogeneity (I² = 59% for depression).

authors: Fincham, G. W., Strauss, C., Montero-Marin, J., & Cavanagh, K.
title: Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials
claim_area: e. Brief digital self-help and exercises
sample/design: Meta-analysis; 12 RCTs (785 adults) for stress, 20 for anxiety, 18 for depression
key finding: Breathwork was associated with lower self-reported stress than controls (g = −0.35, small-to-medium).
limitations: Most trials at moderate risk of bias; authors caution against overstating benefits.

authors: Jabs, M., Thompson, M., Linardon, J., Messer, M., & Wade, T. D.
title: Assessing the effectiveness, adherence and attrition of smartphone-based mental health interventions in university students: A systematic review and meta-analysis
claim_area: e. Brief digital self-help and exercises
sample/design: Multilevel meta-analysis; 122 studies of app-based interventions in university students
key finding: Apps had small effects on anxiety (d = 0.22), depression (d = 0.25) and stress (d = 0.28) and a moderate effect on well-being (d = 0.47), with 17% attrition and 70% adherence.
limitations: Substantial heterogeneity; inconsistent engagement reporting (authors).

authors: Huckvale, K., Torous, J., & Larsen, M. E.
title: Assessment of the data sharing and privacy practices of smartphone apps for depression and smoking cessation
claim_area: f. Privacy, on-device processing and trust
sample/design: Cross-sectional technical audit of 36 top-ranked depression and smoking-cessation apps (US, Australia)
key finding: 33 of 36 apps (92%) transmitted data to third parties and 29 (81%) sent data to Google or Facebook, often without disclosing it.
limitations: Snapshot from 2018; 36 apps in two countries.

authors: Iwaya, L. H., Babar, M. A., Rashid, A., & Wijayarathna, C.
title: On the privacy of mental health apps: An empirical investigation and its implications for app development
claim_area: f. Privacy, on-device processing and trust
sample/design: Static and dynamic privacy analysis of 27 top-ranked Android mental health apps
key finding: The apps showed unnecessary permissions, weak cryptography, leaks of personal data in logs and web requests, and third-party sharing.
limitations: Android only; one point in time.

authors: Melcher, J., & Torous, J.
title: Smartphone apps for college mental health: A concern for privacy and quality of current offerings
claim_area: f. Privacy, on-device processing and trust
sample/design: Review of apps recommended on 60 US college counselling-centre websites (218 unique apps)
key finding: Of the apps still available, 39% had no privacy policy, 49% of those with a policy shared data with third parties, and only 16% had published efficacy studies.
limitations: US counselling centres only; app landscape changes quickly.

authors: Roque, N., & Felt, J.
title: Acceptability of active and passive data collection methods for mobile health research: Cross-sectional survey of an online adult sample in the United States
claim_area: f. Privacy, on-device processing and trust
sample/design: Online survey; N = 1,489 US adults (Prolific)
key finding: People were least willing to share data with high re-identification potential such as GPS, and 71% wanted the ability to delete all their data.
limitations: Online panel, US adults (mean age 35.5), research context rather than a wellbeing app.

authors: Baumel, A., Muench, F., Edan, S., & Kane, J. M.
title: Objective user engagement with mental health apps: Systematic search and panel-based usage analysis
claim_area: g. Risks and criticism
sample/design: Real-world usage panel data for 93 Android mental health apps (≥ 10,000 installs)
key finding: Median retention was 3.9% at day 15 and 3.3% at day 30, and breathing-exercise apps had a median 30-day retention of 0%.
limitations: Android only; aggregated panel data; no outcome data.

authors: Liu, C., Torous, J., Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M., Messer, M., Anderson, C., Soliman, O. M., & Linardon, J.
title: Uptake, adherence, and attrition in clinical trials of depression and anxiety apps: A systematic review and meta-analysis
claim_area: g. Risks and criticism
sample/design: Meta-analysis of 79 RCTs (92 app conditions)
key finding: Even in trials, adherence was 61.8% and attrition 18.6% at post-test and 28.4% at follow-up; attrition was lower with reminders and human contact.
limitations: Trial settings overstate real-world engagement; wide prediction intervals.

authors: Borghouts, J., Eikey, E., Mark, G., De Leon, C., Schueller, S. M., Schneider, M., Stadnick, N., Zheng, K., Mukamel, D., & Sorkin, D. H.
title: Barriers to and facilitators of user engagement with digital mental health interventions: Systematic review
claim_area: g. Risks and criticism
sample/design: Systematic review of 208 articles
key finding: Common barriers to engagement were severe mental health problems, technical issues and lack of personalisation; facilitators included insight into one's health and a sense of control.
limitations: Heterogeneous methods; mostly descriptive.

authors: Astill Wright, L., Monk-Cunliffe, J., Guo, B., & Morriss, R.
title: Adverse events of mood monitoring and ambulatory assessment in depression and bipolar disorder: Systematic review and meta-analysis
claim_area: g. Risks and criticism
sample/design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 77 mood-monitoring studies
key finding: Only 19% of studies reported adverse events; pooled prevalence was 4%, including increased burden or stress (4%) and mood worsening (2%).
limitations: Severe under-reporting, heterogeneity and publication bias; causality could not be inferred (authors); clinical populations.

authors: Munir, S., Dallison, S., Padley, H., Fung, H. M., Perry, G., Hall, C. L., & Loades, M. E.
title: How have contemporary studies evaluating self-help digital mental health interventions for young people monitored and reported on adverse events and harms?: A systematic scoping review
claim_area: g. Risks and criticism
sample/design: Scoping review of 37 studies of self-guided digital interventions for young people (2019–2024)
key finding: Only 12 of 37 studies (32.4%) described how they assessed adverse events, leaving a gap in safety monitoring of self-help tools for young people.
limitations: Scoping review; describes reporting practice, not harm rates.
